sec.title: Background
sec.p: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a leading cause of childhood blindness, with rising incidence as neonatal care improves. Established risk factors include low birth weight, prematurity, and supplemental oxygen, yet current clinical prediction tools have limited early accuracy. The placenta, serving as the maternal-fetal interface, may harbor transcriptomic signatures reflecting intrauterine inflammation and hypoxia that influence ROP development; however, the specific placental genes involved and their predictive value remain largely unknown. This study aimed to identify placenta-derived differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with ROP and construct a predictive risk model integrating gene expression and clinical variables for early ROP diagnosis and prevention.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: DEGs were screened from the GSE218039 placental RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) dataset (ROP vs. control). Functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, and immune infiltration analyses were performed. Overlapping DEGs with the oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) mouse model (GSE200195, GSE158799) were identified. Fourteen upregulated genes were validated by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) in OIR retinal tissues. Elastic-net penalized regression and multivariate logistic regression were applied to the GSE32472 dataset (postnatal days 5 and 28) to select predictive genes and clinical variables (birth weight, bronchopulmonary dysplasia) for constructing a nomogram.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 1,071 DEGs (758 upregulated, 313 downregulated) were identified, enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and chemokine signaling pathways. Seven genes (B2M, C3, ITGAX, CAPG, MCAM, MMP25, LGALS3) were significantly upregulated in OIR retinas (P<0.05). Neutrophil infiltration was increased in ROP and positively correlated with these genes. Four overlapping genes (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, B2M) were selected from both time points and combined with birth weight and bronchopulmonary dysplasia to build a nomogram. The model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.948 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.899–0.998] on postnatal day 5, with good calibration.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The nomogram incorporating four placenta-derived genes and clinical variables shows excellent predictive performance for early ROP detection, offering a potential tool for individualized risk assessment, early intervention, and prevention of ROP in premature infants.

sec.title: Key findings
sec.p: • A novel prediction model was established based on four genes (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, B2M) associated with retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) and clinical variables.

sec.title: What is known and what is new?
sec.p: • Existing evidence indicates that the pathophysiology of the mother and the placenta affects the occurrence and development of ROP, but the molecular mechanism remains unclear.
• Key differentially expressed genes (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, B2M) related to ROP were identified in placental tissue, and a predictive model for ROP was constructed by integrating clinical variables.

sec.title: What is the implication, and what should change now?
sec.p: • Studies suggest that placenta-derived genes may serve as potential therapeutic targets and contribute to basic research on ROP. Next steps should include validating the predictive model in a prospective clinical cohort and experimentally confirming the key genes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is an ocular disorder in preterm infants, responsible for 40% of blindness in children on a global scale (1). This condition is defined by incomplete development of the retinal vascular system and the occurrence of pathological neovascularization. Key independent risk factors associated with ROP include low birth weight (BW) (<1,500 g), gestational age (<32 weeks),and exposure to supplemental oxygen after birth. Although additional risk factors have been identified—such as maternal health, prenatal and perinatal conditions, breastfeeding practices, and nutritional intake (2)—the implementation of preventive measures has not been adequate to eliminate the risk of ROP. The effects of ROP impose significant health challenges and economic strain, highlighting the need for effective prevention and treatment methodologies. The progression of ROP is divided into two distinct phases: the ischemic phase, which is characterized by hindered retinal capillary development and the regression of existing blood vessels, driven by both neonatal and extrinsic factors, and the proliferative phase, which is defined by the growth of retinal neovascularization originating from ischemic areas devoid of blood vessels (Figure 1) (3). Timely intervention during the initial “preclinical” phase may foster proper retinal vascular development and avert advancement to the subsequent phase.

caption.p: Pathophysiology of retinopathy of prematurity. Two stages of ROP development and the main pathophysiological mechanisms. Retinal blood vessels begin to grow from the 14–16 weeks of postmenstrual age, developing from the papilla to the periphery of the retina, reaching the nasal side of the retina around 36 weeks of postmenstrual age, and reaching the temporal side of the retina around 40 weeks of postmenstrual age; in premature infants, retinal vascularization is incomplete at birth, leaving avascular areas that form the basis of ROP. sec.p: The environment within the uterus and the placenta plays an increasingly significant role in determining the susceptibility to and protection against diseases in premature infants. Acting as the primary connection for maternal-fetal interactions, the placenta facilitates the exchange of nutrients and oxygen (4). Maternal physiological and pathological alterations can influence the fetus through the placenta. For instance, research indicates that maternal inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and immune cells associated with chorioamnionitis are elevated and can be found in fetal tissues (such as fetal membranes) and umbilical cord blood (5).Investigations have revealed a strong link between placental abnormalities and unfavorable neonatal outcomes, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), ROP, sepsis, and patent ductus arteriosus (6-10). Early studies, for example, connected inflammation-related placental changes induced by intrauterine inflammation to a heightened risk of ROP (10-13). Moreover, studies have found that higher levels of inflammatory proteins in the systemic circulation of premature infants at birth increase the risk of developing ROP, whereas higher levels of angiogenic and neurotrophic factors may confer protective effects (14). The ability to predict ROP risk in premature infants through testing of placental tissue, amniotic fluid, or cord blood may allow for effective preventive strategies, consequently decreasing the incidence of ROP.

This research employed bioinformatics techniques to pinpoint differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with ROP using datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), which were subsequently validated via quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). We developed a predictive risk scoring model for ROP by combining elastic net penalized regression with multiple logistic regression analysis and clinical data, offering insight for personalized ROP diagnosis and preventive strategies. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD and ARRIVE reporting checklists (available at https://tp.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tp-2026-0544/rc).

sec.title: The collection of online data
sec.p: All four datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). GSE218039 contains 30 RNA-seq samples from human placental tissues (14 ROP cases and 16 controls), sequenced on the Illumina platform. GSE200195 and GSE158799 are RNA-seq datasets derived from retinal tissues of the mouse oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) model; GSE200195 was generated on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform (GPL13112) and covers five time points from postnatal day (P)12 to P16, whereas GSE158799 was generated on the Ion Torrent Proton platform (GPL18635) and corresponds to the P17 time point. GSE32472 is a microarray dataset based on the Affymetrix Human Gene 1.0 ST Array platform (GPL6244), profiling whole‑genome expression in peripheral blood leukocytes from very low birth weight (VLBW, BW <1,500 g) preterm infants. The original study initially enrolled 120 preterm infants, of whom 111 completed microarray profiling at at least one time point. Blood samples were collected on postnatal days 5, 14, and 28. ROP diagnosis was established by experienced ophthalmologists using binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy according to the International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ICROP). A total of 97 infants had both day-5 blood samples and complete ROP status information, comprising 51 no-ROP and 46 ROP cases. The original submitted metadata for GSE32472 did not contain detailed ROP staging information (e.g., zone, stage, plus disease) for individual patients; therefore, grouping into “ROP” versus “no ROP” was based on the binary clinical labels provided in the original study, precluding further sub‑classification into type 1 or type 2 ROP. This represents an inherent limitation of using this public dataset. It should be noted that the three transcriptomic datasets (GSE218039, GSE200195, and GSE158799) were integrated using an “overlap screening” strategy rather than a pooled analysis. Each dataset underwent independent internal normalization and differential expression analysis (DESeq2 normalization for GSE218039 and GSE200195, and the platform-specific normalization pipeline for GSE158799), followed by intersection of the resulting DEG lists at the gene symbol level. Given the substantial differences across the three datasets in species (human vs. mouse), tissue origin (placenta vs. retina), and sequencing platform (Illumina vs. Ion Torrent), direct cross‑dataset batch correction was not considered biologically justified. Accordingly, we did not perform batch correction across datasets; instead, differential expression analysis was conducted within each dataset individually (ROP/OIR vs. respective controls), and cross‑dataset selection was achieved by taking the intersection of gene symbols. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments.

sec.title: Analysis of datasets and DEGs screening
sec.p: The initial preprocessing of raw data from the GSE218039 dataset was conducted. To eliminate non-informative transcripts, genes with a mean read count of less than 10 across all samples were excluded, utilizing the “dplyr” package in R (version 4.3.2). Following this, the “DESeq2” package was employed to detect DEGs (15). Genes with a P value of less than 0.05 and a |log2 fold change (FC)| greater than 0.585 were classified as DEGs in the GSE218039 dataset. For enhanced visualization of these DEGs, a volcano plot was generated using the “EnhancedVolcano” package in R software. Applying the same criteria for P value and log2 FC, the analysis of validation sets GSE200195 and GSE158799 led to the identification of upregulated DEGs. The shared genes were then analyzed for a longitudinal comparison of RNA expression profiles across these datasets, culminating in the creation of a cluster diagram that integrates log2 FC.

sec.title: Gene enrichment analysis and Disease Ontology analysis
sec.p: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) Pathway analysis, and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) were conducted utilizing the “clusterProfiler” package within R software (16). Gene enrichment assessments relied on an adjusted P value threshold of <0.01, while visualization utilized the “ggplot2” package in R. Additionally, the analysis of Disease Ontology for DEGs was performed with the “DOSE” package inR (17), considering terms with an adjusted P value of <0.05 to be significantly enriched.

sec.title: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis
sec.p: Through cross-tissue integration of transcriptomic data from human placenta (GSE218039) and mouse OIR models (GSE200195, GSE158799), we identified genes that exhibited expression at a minimum of five time points (placenta, P12–P16 and P17) and subsequently explored their potential molecular functions, we based on the STRING database (https://string-db.org/) constructed a PPI network. The PPI network was visualized using Cytoscape software (version 3.9.0), and a Benjamini-Hochberg corrected P value <0.05 was used as a threshold to screen for significant interactions.

sec.title: Construction of the OIR model
sec.p: C57BL/6J mice were obtained from the Hunan SJA Laboratory Animal Center (Changsha, China). Experiments were performed under a project license (No. NCULAE-20251028001) granted by the Animal Experimentation Ethics Committee of Jiangxi Medical College, Nanchang University, in compliance with institutional guidelines for the care and use of animals. The OIR model was induced in C57BL/6J mice following the protocol originally established by Smith et al. (18) and subsequently refined by Connor et al. (19). On postnatal day 7 (P7), maternal mice and their pups were placed in a hyperoxic chamber with an oxygen concentration of 75%±2% for 5 consecutive days. On P12, they were returned to normoxic room air conditions. Mice at postnatal day 17 (P17) were euthanized by isoflurane inhalation; the eyeballs were enucleated and retinal tissues were dissected for subsequent experiments. During OIR modeling, health status was monitored twice daily. No unexpected adverse events or unscheduled deaths occurred. Humane intervention criteria (≥20% body weight loss, severe lethargy, or dyspnea) were predefined, and no animal reached these endpoints.

sec.title: mRNA isolation and quantitative real-time (qRT) PCR
sec.p: Among the genes expressed at ≥5 time points (placenta, P12–P17), we further selected those that were upregulated and highly expressed at multiple time points. Candidate genes closely related to retinal neovascularization or ROP were identified through literature review and subsequently validated by qRT-PCR. Total RNA was purified from retina using TRIzol (Invitrogen, CA, USA), quantified by NanoDrop (NanoDrop Technologies, DE, USA), and reverse-transcribed into cDNA with HiScript II Q RT SuperMix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). Real-time PCR was performed on a StepOnePlus™ system (Applied Biosystems, CA, USA) using SYBR Green. Target gene expression was normalized to β-actin and analyzed using the 2−ΔΔCt method. The following primer sequences were employed in this study. C3: 5'-AGAAGCGTCTCCATCAAGATTCC-3' (forward), 5'-ACCACTGTCACGTACTTGTGC-3' (reverse); IL1R1: 5'-GTGCTACTGGGGCT CATTTGT-3' (forward), 5'-GGAGTAAGA GGACACTTGCGAAT-3' (reverse); LGALS3: 5'-GGAGAGGGAATGATGTTGCCT-3' (forward), 5'-TCCTGCTTCGTGTTACACACA-3' (reverse); MCAM: 5'-AAGCTGGTCACTTTAACCACC-3' (forward), 5'-ATTCACTCTTACGAGTCGGGG; MMP19: 5'-GCTGACATTCGCCTCTCTTTC-3' (forward), 5'-CACTCCTTGATAGGTCCCCTC-3' (reverse); MMP25: 5'-CTCCTGCCCGTCTCTA CTACC-3' (forward), 5'-GACCTTCGCATCGGG ATTCTG-3' (reverse); CAPG: 5'-GCTCTAC CAGGTTAAGGGGAA-3' (forward), 5'-GGC AAAGATGTTCTGACCCAG-3' (reverse); CCR5: 5'-ATGGATTTTCAAGGGTCAGTTCC-3' (forward), 5'-CTGAGCCGCAATTTGTTTCAC-3' (reverse); HK2: 5'-GTGTGCTCCGAGTAAGGGTG-3' (forward), 5'-CAGGCATTCGGCAATGTGG-3' (reverse); IL1RL2: 5'-GAAACAAACGGGGCAGTAAATC-3' (forward), 5'-GGTGAACTCTAAGGTGTCTGTTG-3' (reverse); ITGAX: 5'-CCAAGACATCGTGTTCCTGATT-3′ (forward), 5'-ACAGCTTTAACAAAGTCCAGCA-3' (reverse); SERPING1: 5'-CACCAACCATAAG ATCCGCAA-3' (forward), 5'GGCACTCAAGTAGACA GCATT-3' (reverse); IRF8: 5'-AGACCATGTTC CGTATCCCCT-3' (forward), 5'-CACAGCGTAAC CTCGTCTTCC-3' (reverse); B2M: 5'-TTCTGGTGCT TGTCTCACTGA-3' (forward), 5'-CAGTATGTT CGGCTTCCCATTC-3' (reverse); β-actin: 5'-GGCTGTATTCCCCTCCATCG-3' (forward), 5'-CCAGTTGGTAACAATGCCATGT-3' (reverse). qRT-PCR data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism software. For each gene, the relative expression level was calculated as the FC (2−ΔΔCt) relative to the internal control β-actin. All experimental samples represented independent biological replicates (n=6 per group, i.e., six individual mice per condition), not technical replicates. Normality and homogeneity of variances were assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Levene’s test, respectively, prior to statistical testing. Differences between the OIR and normoxic control groups were evaluated using two-tailed Student’s t-test for normally distributed data with equal variances; otherwise, the Mann-Whitney U test was applied as a non-parametric alternative. Given the exploratory nature of this validation (14 genes tested in a single animal model), we acknowledge that no adjustment for multiple comparisons [e.g., false discovery rate (FDR) correction] was applied; therefore, the results should be interpreted with caution, and the P values are reported uncorrected.

sec.title: Evaluation and correlation analysis of infiltration-related immune cells
sec.p: The types and proportions of infiltrating immune cells associated with the validated genes in GSE218039 were estimated using the “CIBERSORT” package (20). Subsequently, the data was visualized using the “corrplot” package in R software. Box plots were generated to illustrate the differential expression levels of immune infiltrating cells between the ROP group and the control group. Spearman correlation coefficient analysis was conducted to demonstrate the relationships between each validated gene and the immune cells. The correlation matrix was then visualized using the “ggplot2” package in R software. Immune cell infiltration was estimated using the CIBERSORT algorithm with the LM22 signature matrix, which was originally derived from purified leukocyte subsets in peripheralblood (20). Although LM22 was not specifically designed for placental tissue, this approach has been widely applied in published studies analyzing placental transcriptomic data across various pregnancy-related conditions, including preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction and gestational diabetes mellitus (21-23). Nevertheless, the resulting estimates should be interpreted with caution, as LM22 does not fully capture the transcriptional signatures of placenta-resident immune populations (e.g., decidual NK cells, Hofbauer cells) or non-immune placental components (24).

sec.title: Construction and evaluation of prediction model
sec.p: To enhance clinical utility, we performed elastic net penalized regression and multivariate logistic regression on the qRT-PCR-validated upregulated and highly expressed genes using the GSE32472 peripheral blood data. Genes that overlapped at both time A and time C were retained, and combined with the time A clinical variables from the same dataset to develop an ROP prediction model. The loss function of elastic-net regression incorporates the regularization strategies of Lasso and Ridge regression, and the penalty strength is jointly controlled by the regularization parameter λ and the mixing parameter ρ (25). In this study, the “caret” (v7.0-1) (26) and “glmnet” (v4.1–10) (27) packages in R were employed to select the optimal combination of λ and ρ, and predictive genes and clinical variables were screened in the GSE32472 dataset. Subsequently, the final prediction model was determined using multivariate logistic regression. A comprehensive nomogram was developed based on the risk scores of the predictive genes and clinical variables, and the model’s predictive performance was assessed through calibration analysis alongside receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve evaluation (28,29). All statistical analyses were conducted using R software, with the applied packages including “glmnet”, “caret”, “rms”, “pROC” and “ggplot2” (30).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All analyses were performed using relevant packages in R (version 4.3.2). For continuous variables that followed a normal distribution and had homogeneous variances, differences between two groups were assessed using the independent samples t-test, and correlations between two variables were evaluated using Pearson correlation analysis. For data that did not meet normality assumptions or exhibited unequal variances, the Wilcoxon ranksum test was used for group comparisons, and Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient was employed for correlation analyses. Statistical significance was defined as a P value <0.05, with P values summarized as follows: not significant (ns), P≥0.05; *, 0.01≤P<0.05; **, 0.001≤P<0.01; ***, 0.0001≤P<0.001.

sec.title: Differential expression of ROP-related genes
sec.p: A total of 1,071 genes that showed DEGs were discovered when comparing the ROP group to the non-ROP group, comprising 758 genes that were upregulated and 313 genesthat were downregulated, as shown in the volcano plot (Figure 2A). The top 10 upregulated genes included AHNAK2, CHRNE, ENKUR, IGFBP1, NOD2, PLAC8, PTGES, PTK2B, RTN4RL2 and TLE6, while the top 10 downregulated genes included ABCC6, AQP11, ENSG00000278384, FABP4, HSPA6, IQCM, ITGA11, MUC4, NR4A1 and TM4SF18 (ranked by adjusted P value).

The orange dots represent the differential expression genes that satisfy both P value and log2 FC, while the dots on the right represent significantly up-regulated genes and the dots on the left represent down-regulated genes. (B) GO enrichment analysis of ROP-related genes. Different colors represent the terms of biological process, cellular component, and molecular function, respectively. sec.title: GO function and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis
sec.p: Cluster analysis of DEGs was performed to evaluate their biological processes and signaling pathways. GO analysis revealed significant enrichment in terms related to positive regulation of cytokine production and cytokine receptor activity (Figure 2B). KEGG analysis identified significantly upregulated pathways involving cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (ACVR1C, CCL4, CCR2, CCR5, CXCL10, IL1R1, IL1R2, TNFSF14, XCL1, XCR1) and chemokine signaling (ADCY7, CCL4, CCR2, CCR5, CXCL10, GNB5, PIK3R1, STAT1, XCL1, XCR1). Downregulated pathways involved glandular tissue dysfunction and the PI3K-AKT pathway related to biomacromolecule metabolism(Figure 2C).

sec.title: GSEA and Disease Ontology analysis
sec.p: GSEA identified 10 gene sets with significant activation and suppression based on adjusted P value and normalized enrichment score cutoffs (Figure 2D). The primary enriched pathways identified were “Cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction”, “Chemokine signaling pathway” and “NOD-like receptor signaling pathway” which aligns with the analyses from GO and KEGG (Figure 2E). The disease ontology evaluation revealed terms that showed a positive correlation with ROP, including primary immunodeficiency disease, anterior uveitis, and panuveitis (Figure 2F). This suggests that the DEGs related to ROP exhibit enrichment in processes associated with the eye, inflammation, and other pathways.

sec.title: Construction of PPI network and identification of consecutive upregulated-DEGs
sec.p: By cross‑tissue intersection of placental‑derived data (GSE218039) and OIR model datasets (GSE200195, GSE158799), we identified 75 DEGs that were expressed at least at five time points (placenta and P12–P17). PPI analysis of these 75 DEGs revealed a network containing 41 nodes and their interactions (Figure 3A,3B). The hub genes included B2M, CCR5, IRF8, ITGAX, CD34, CD93, TIE1, MMRN2, ROBO4, and PTPRB (Figure 3C). From the above 75 DEGs, we further screened 36 DEGs that were consistently upregulated at multiple time points, and generated a cluster heatmap to display the differential expression patterns between the ROP and non-ROP groups (Figure 3D).

sec.title: Validation of upregulated ROP-related DEGs in OIR group
sec.p: Based on a literature review, we selected 14 genes that were closely associated with retinal neovascularization or ROP and performed qRT-PCR validation in the OIR model. As shown in Figure 3E, B2M, C3, ITGAX, CAPG, MCAM, MMP25, and LGALS3 were significantly increased in OIR samples compared to normal retinal samples (P<0.05).

sec.title: The correlation between validated genes and immune cell infiltration levels
sec.p: To assess the impact of seven validated genes on disease pathogenesis, the CIBERSORT analysis tool calculated the proportion of leukocyte subpopulations from 22 types of blood sources in the ROP and control groups. Based on tissue expression differences, non-expressed and low expressed subpopulations were excluded from the results. Analysis of the immune microenvironment revealed notable variations in the abundance of six immune cells, including, NK cells resting, T cells CD4 naïve, T cells CD8, B cells naïve, T cells CD4 memory resting, and Neutrophils (Figure 4A). Specifically, the infiltration level of neutrophils in the ROP group was significantly higher than that in the control group, whereas the infiltration of lymphocytes (including B cells, NK cells, and T cells) showed lower infiltration in the ROP group. No significant difference in monocyte infiltration was observed between the two groups. Then, the spearman correlation coefficient between validated genes and the infiltration level of the immune cell was calculated. The correlation analysis revealed that the inferred abundance of neutrophils was positively correlated with the expression of C3, ITGAX, MCAM, MMP25, and LGALS3, while the inferred abundance of resting CD4+ memory T cells was negatively correlated with C3, ITGAX, MCAM, CAPG, and MMP25 (Figure 4B). These findings suggest a potential association between placental immune cell composition and the expression of the validated genes, which is consistent with previous reports linking the peripheral blood neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) to ROP severity (31). However, it should be emphasized that the present analysis was based on CIBERSORT deconvolution of placental tissue and does not directly measure circulating immune cell counts; therefore, the inferred associations should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, requiring validation in paired placental and blood samples using flow cytometry or complete blood counts in future studies.

caption.p: Immune cell infiltration analysis. (A) Violin plot of the abundance of seven type of immune cell infiltration in the in the ROP and non-ROP groups. Significant differences were defined by a P value, *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001. (B) Correlation graph representing the association of immune cells with seven validated genes. NK, natural killer; ROP, retinopathy of prematurity.

sec.title: Construction of a multivariate prediction model for individual disease risk
sec.p: To further enhance clinical feasibility, we constructed a comprehensive predictive model using multivariate logistic regression based on data from two time points (time A and time C) in the GSE32472 dataset. Time A refers to postnatal day 5, when ROP has not yet developed or is in its early stages, whereas time C refers to postnatal day 28, which typically corresponds to the peak incidence of ROP and pathological neovascularization. As shown in Figure 5A,5B, we applied elastic‑net penalized regression to screen for genes among those upregulated in the OIR model at both time A and time C. Four overlapping genes (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, and B2M) were identified at both time points and used to generate a risk score(Figure 5C). The risk score was calculated as follows: Risk score = −0.1057 + 0.1357*B2M + 0.1145*CAPG + 0.1397*MCAM + 0.2656*MMP25. To further optimize the ROP prediction model, we incorporated the risk score of the four genes together with clinical variables from the GSE32472 dataset, including BW and BPD, to construct a nomogram (Figure 5D,5E). As illustrated in Figure 5F, the nomogram developed on postnatal day 5 showed remarkable predictive accuracy, achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.948 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.899–0.998] for both sensitivity and specificity. Concurrently, the analysis of the calibration curve (Figure 5G)revealed a favorable correlation between the predicted probabilities and the actual observed values. The bias-corrected curve closely adhered to the ideal diagonal reference line, suggesting that this model provided trustworthy predictions. (A detailed flowchart of the gene screening process is provided in Figure S1).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: ROP is the most common cause of vision loss in premature infants worldwide. Despite extensive research into ROP pathogenesis, the maternal environment’s role and fetal systemic changes in ROP onset and progression remain largely unexplored. ROP is not an isolated ocular disease but rather a local manifestation of systemic vascular dysplasia and inflammatory dysregulation in premature infants (32). The placenta, serving as both a “filter” for fetal circulation and a “signal hub” for maternal-fetal interaction, undergoes transcriptomic changes that collectively reflect the global intrauterine stress (hypoxia, inflammation, oxidative stress) experienced by the fetus, thereby constituting a “molecular record” of the fetal systemic health status (33,34). The retina, as a terminal target organ, develops pathological neovascularization as a local consequence of the same systemic pathological process. Peripheral blood leukocytes, acting as circulating “sensors”, dynamically reflect and sustain the systemic inflammatory state through their gene expression profiles (14,35). Thus, the placenta, retina, and peripheral blood represent distinct observational windows into the same disease process, rather than isolated biological entities.

In this study, the DEGs identified from human placental data and mouse OIR model data are key regulators of lymphocyte trafficking and cytokine signaling, all encoding proteins involved in inflammatory immune responses, cytoskeletal remodeling, and transmembrane signal transduction—pathways that are highly conserved across mammals (36-39). Subsequently, the OIR mouse model was used for pathophysiological validation of the DEGs. The identified genes were not only statistically significant but also functionally relevant to the hallmark neovascularization and inflammatory processes characteristic of ROP. Finally, a prediction model was constructed using peripheral blood from preterm infants. The placental gene expression profile serves as a “cumulative molecular imprint” of the chronic pathological stress (especially inflammation and hypoxia) experienced by the fetus in utero (40,41). The immune cell functional status and systemic inflammatory propensity programmed by intrauterine exposure to inflammation and hypoxia do not disappear immediately at birth but persist into the early postnatal period and are continuously reflected in the transcriptome of circulating leukocytes (42,43). The differential expression of the four core genes in the GSE32472 dataset as early as postnatal day 5 in peripheral blood provides preliminary evidence for this “intrauterine programming-postnatal continuation” hypothesis. Therefore, the shared gene expression signatures observed across placenta, retina, and peripheral blood reflect the coordinated transcriptional response of the same systemic pathological process across different tissues (44).

In this study, we identified 1,071 DEGs related to ROP from placental tissue transcriptomic datasets, to further clarify the possible biological roles of the DEGs, additional functional enrichment analysis was conducted. This analysis revealed that the interaction between cytokines and their receptors, along with chemokine signaling pathways, plays a vital role in the development of ROP. Consistent with our findings, Xiao et al. reported significant enrichment of cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathways in the context of inflammation and immune response using a zebrafish uveitis model (45). Beyond inflammation, this pathway has also been implicated in angiogenic processes; for instance, Varinská et al. demonstrated that galectin-8 promotes VEGF-induced angiogenesis through in vitro and in vivo models (46), and Ji et al. found that microRNA-296 mediates corneal neovascularization in a mouse model of corneal alkali burns (47). Chemokines, essential for leukocyte migration during hematopoiesis and inflammation (48), are significantly expressed in retinal vascular dysfunction (49), potentially influencing age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (50,51). These findings suggest a correlation between maternal placental inflammation and immune response and retinal vascular or neovascularization in premature newborns.

Through cross‑tissue intersection of placental data (GSE218039) and OIR model datasets (GSE200195, GSE158799), we identified 75 DEGs that were expressed at least at five time points (placenta, P12–P16 and P17). To explore the underlying molecular mechanisms, we performed PPI network analysis and identified 10 hub genes. CD34 and CCR5 are involved in ROP or pathological neovascularization progression, while the roles of other hub genes in ROP warrant further investigation. Siemerink et al. (52) demonstrated reduced pathological retinal extraretinal neovascular clusters in CD34-deficient mice. CCR5, a beta chemokine receptor family member, is expressed by T cells and macrophages (53). Bosco et al. (53)observed significant CCR5 expression in bone marrow-derived mononuclear cells in the P17 OIR retina. ITGAX plays a crucial role in facilitating interactions between cells during inflammatory responses, especially concerning the adhesion and chemotaxis of monocytes, and its expression is notably increased in a mouse model of diabetic retinopathy (DR) (54). IRF8 is involved in inflammatory and apoptotic processes (55), crucial for suppressing retinal inflammation and choroidal neovascularization (CNV) (56). Liu et al. (57)found B2M, C3, and SERPING1 upregulated in all AMD stages in humans and an AMD mouse model. Diabetic retinopathy (58) and AMD (59) are both retinal microvascular diseases that lead to retinal neovascularization and increased vascular permeability, which are similar to the pathological manifestations of ROP neovascularization. These genes, involved in retinal microvascular diseases, suggest potential value in ROP research and provide new therapeutic targets.

Based on the above 75 DEGs, we further screened 36 genes that were consistently upregulated and highly expressed at multiple time points. Through literature review, 14 genes closely associated with retinal neovascularization or ROP were identified and subjected to qRT-PCR validation. Seven genes (B2M, C3, ITGAX, CAPG, MCAM, MMP25, and LGALS3) were significantly upregulated in OIR retinas (P<0.05), suggesting that these genes may be involved in the pathological processes of retinal neovascularization. To further explore the potential link between the validated genes and the immune microenvironment, we estimated the immune cell composition of placental tissues using the CIBERSORT deconvolution algorithm. The analysis revealed a higher inferred abundance of neutrophils in the ROP group compared to the control group, whereas lymphocyte subsets (including B cells, NK cells, and T cells) showed a contrasting pattern. These findings are consistent with previous studies demonstrating that neutrophils play a critical role in the pathogenesis of OIR. Deliyanti et al. reported that early neutrophil infiltration in OIR drives the retina toward a pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic state, ultimately contributing to severe retinal vascular damage (60). Additionally, clinical evidence has suggested that peripheral blood inflammatory indicators, such as the Delta Neutrophil Index (DNI) and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), are associated with ROP risk and severity (31,61). However, it should be emphasized that the immune cell proportions presented here were derived from computational deconvolution of placental bulk RNA-seq data using the LM22 signature matrix, which was originally constructed from peripheral blood leukocytes (20). This approach has inherent limitations when applied to placental tissue, as it does not fully capture the transcriptional signatures of placenta-resident immune populations (e.g., decidual NK cells, Hofbauer cells) or account for the non-immune components (e.g., trophoblast, stroma) that dominate placental tissue (24). Therefore, the inferred immune cell abundances should be interpreted as exploratory evidence rather than definitive measurements. The observed correlation between the seven validated genes and the inferred neutrophil abundance is consistent with the known roles of these genes in inflammatory responses, but the direct extrapolation from placental deconvolution data to peripheral blood NLR is not supported by our current dataset and would require validation in paired samples using flow cytometry or complete blood counts in future studies.

To improve clinical applicability, we performed elastic net penalized regression analysis on the seven qRT-PCR-validated genes using the GSE32472 peripheral blood dataset. Four genes (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, and B2M) that consistently overlapped at both postnatal day 5 and day 28 were ultimately included, along with clinical variables from the GSE32472 dataset at postnatal day 5 (such as BW and BPD), to construct a prediction model for ROP. The model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.948 (95% CI: 0.899–0.998), indicating strong predictive performance. Currently, widely used clinical ROP risk prediction tools—such as WINROP (62), CHOPROP (63), ROPScore (63,64), G-ROP (64), and DIGIROP-Birth (65)—mainly rely on clinical parameters including BW, gestational age, and postnatal weight gain rate. The predictive performance (AUC) of these models typically ranges between 0.75 and 0.85, suggesting that incorporating placenta‑derived genes may provide predictive gains beyond traditional clinical variables. The gene markers identified in this study also offer several potential advantages over clinical variables. First, the timewindow advantage: placenta-derived DEGs reflect the intrauterine exposure to hypoxia and inflammation experienced by the fetus, and can provide ROP risk information at or even before birth (33). In contrast, traditional clinical variables (such as duration of oxygen therapy and weight gain rate) depend on the postnatal clinical course, making it difficult to achieve truly “early” prediction. Second, mechanistic insights: the four genes identified in this study (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, and B2M) are all involved in core pathological processes of ROP, including inflammatory responses, immune cell chemotaxis, and angiogenesis (66-69). Their expression levels directly reflect the biological nature of the disease, rather than merely serving as surrogate risk factors. Third, early intervention window: the expression levels of these genes can be measured in peripheral blood as early as postnatal day 5, providing a possible time window for implementing preventive interventions before ROP progresses into the proliferative phase (1).

Moreover, these genes might act as important references for upcoming clinical investigations. MCAM, also known as CD146, has been shown to be involved in angiogenesis and inflammatory responses, along with its soluble form (70).Moreover, several studies have demonstrated that antiCD146 antibodies can reduce pathological retinal neovascularization in the OIR model (71,72). CAPG is an actin‑binding protein that influences endothelial cell migration by regulating actin cytoskeleton reorganization. Studies have shown that CAPG plays a critical role in angiogenesis and migration, and that targeting CAPG with the vascular disrupting agent DMXAA can effectively suppress endothelial cell angiogenic capacity (67,73). B2M (β2-microglobulin) is an active pro-angiogenic molecule, and multiple studies have confirmed its ability to promote angiogenesis (68). For instance, in multiple myeloma (MM), B2M levels are positively correlated with proangiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2) (74,75). Liu et al. found that B2M expression was increased at all stages of AMD (57). MMP25 is a membrane-bound GPI-anchored protease (76,77) involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, protein degradation, and inflammatory processes, including neutrophil migration to sites of inflammation (78,79). Recent studies have identified MMP25 as a key regulator of organspecific angiogenesis (80). San et al. reported that reducing MMP25 expression may delay pathological vascular remodeling (39).

The four gene markers are amenable to qRT-PCR detection from peripheral blood, a technique that is straightforward and costcontrolled, and widely available in hospitals with basic molecular biology setups. As previous work suggests that minimally invasive sampling and robust biomarkers are advantageous for neonatal care (81,82), our model appears to have a solid foundation for clinical deployment from both a technical and an economic standpoint.

Notably, the original study design of the GSE32472 dataset was primarily focused on BPD, with ROP recorded as a secondary clinical variable. In this cohort, the prevalence of BPD was 61% (68/111) and that of ROP was 45% (50/111), indicating a high degree of comorbidity between these two conditions in VLBW preterm infants (83).This comorbidity arises from the fact that BPD and ROP share multiple risk factors, including extremely low gestational age, VLBW, oxygen therapy exposure, and systemic inflammation (83). This overlap has certain implications for our study. On one hand, gene expression signals from shared pathophysiological pathways between BPD and ROP may be captured simultaneously in this dataset, which explains why the four core genes (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, and B2M) are all enriched in the common pathways of inflammation and angiogenesis (84-86). On the other hand, we cannot exclude the possibility that some of the DEGs primarily reflect “BPD‑associated inflammation” rather than “ROP-specific signals”. Therefore, what our model essentially predicts may be the “risk of systemic inflammation-related complications in preterm infants” rather than strictly ROP-specific risk. This limitation suggests that future studies should adjust for BPD status in independent prospective cohorts to evaluate the independent predictive value of this gene signature for ROP. At the same time, the objective comorbidity between BPD and ROP also implies that intervention strategies targeting the shared inflammatoryangiogenic pathways may have the potential to reduce the incidence of both diseases simultaneously, which holds important clinical translational significance (84).

Nevertheless, several limitations exist in our study. First, the analyses rely solely on retrospective data from publicly available databases, and no prospective validation has been performed using external clinical cohorts. Second, experimental evidence from in vitro or in vivo studies is lacking to verify the expression levels and specific biological functions of the core genes. Future investigations should prioritize targeted prospective studies to assess the model’s predictive accuracy (sensitivity and specificity), clinical utility, and practical feasibility, as well as to further clarify the molecular mechanisms underlying the role of these genes in the pathogenesis and progression of ROP. This study cannot directly establish a causal link between the DEGs identified in the placenta and retinal neovascularization across tissues, nor can we rule out the possibility that some overlapping genes are merely epiphenomena of the inflammatory response rather than true drivers of pathology. Clarification of these issues will require future studies employing longitudinal models integrating the placenta-circulation-retina axis, or organoid co‑culture systems, to directly verify the causal chain among the three compartments.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, we successfully identified placenta-derived DEGs associated with ROP and constructed a robust predictive risk model integrating four key genes (MMP25, CAPG, MCAM, and B2M) with clinical variables including BW and BPD. The nomogram demonstrated excellent early predictive performance (AUC =0.948) as early as postnatal day 5, offering a potential tool for individualized risk stratification and early intervention in preterm infants. Our findings also highlight the systemic nature of ROP, linking placental inflammation, immune dysregulation, and retinal neovascularization through conserved molecular pathways. While further prospective validation and mechanistic studies are warranted, this gene-clinical integrated model provides a promising foundation for advancing early diagnosis, personalized management, and ultimately prevention of ROP in vulnerable neonatal populations.
